title: New Data Shows Building Knowledge Can Boost Reading Comprehension
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler reports on a University of Pennsylvania randomized trial of ARC Core, a science-based literacy curriculum, with over 1,500 kindergartners in 21 Philadelphia public schools. Children who got it scored 0.17 of a standard deviation higher on reading comprehension, larger than the effects in an earlier Florida State study of Core Knowledge Language Arts, and showed a 0.32 effect on motivation to read. She argues this adds to evidence against teaching comprehension as a set of transferable skills and strategies, since strategy instruction stops helping after about six sessions. She also notes the limits: few comparable kindergarten studies, unknown durability, and a control group that got more science than expected. She closes on the need for teacher support when integrating literacy and content.
points: A year of content-focused kindergarten literacy produced a 0.17 standard deviation comprehension gain, far above the typical 0.01 effect for kindergarten trials.
Reading strategy instruction stops adding benefit after about six sessions, yet schools drill skills for years while squeezing out science and social studies.
Both genders gained in motivation to read (0.32), and boys benefited more in comprehension, which matters for high-poverty urban settings.
Caveats are stated plainly: few comparable studies, uncertain persistence of effects, and a control group that already received substantial science instruction.
Teachers need professional support to integrate literacy and content, because the approach departs from what many learned in education schools.
quotes: Studies have repeatedly shown that readers who have knowledge of the topic they’re reading about are better able to understand the text. There’s also evidence that reading comprehension scores are highly correlated with general cultural knowledge, suggesting that the more knowledge you have, the better you can understand whatever you read.

But that evidence also shows that students stop benefiting after only six sessions of instruction. We routinely teach “skills and strategies”—including many that have no evidence behind them—day after day, for years, while marginalizing other subjects like social studies and science that could build academic knowledge.

The children who got ARC Core did significantly better on a standardized test of reading comprehension—0.17 of a standard deviation, in research-speak. That may not sound like much, but it’s even larger than the effects found by the Florida researchers—0.06 and 0.12—and they were surprised by the magnitude of their results.
In past years, I would not have [seen] more than half my room reading,” one teacher told researchers. “This year, it’s 100% reading, down to my lowest reader.

Still, the study is an important addition to the growing body of evidence suggesting that if we want to improve reading outcomes, combining literacy instruction with knowledge-building is the way to go. One of the Florida researchers, Sonia Cabell, recently co-authored an analysis of 35 different studies of that approach at the elementary level.

Cabell also made the important point that many teachers need professional support to do a good job of integrating literacy instruction with knowledge—the kind of support teachers in the ARC Core study received from ARC staff. Not only is the approach different from what teachers are used to, it also departs from what many learned about literacy instruction at schools of education. Integrating literacy and content instruction can be difficult, Cabell said—but it can also be powerful.
